1G (Number Theory)

Words: 264 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 264
1G OurBigBook.com
The Lagrange root bound over a field says that a nonzero polynomial of degree r over a field has at most r roots. In particular, a polynomial modular congruence of degree r modulo a prime number has at most r incongruent solutions unless all its coefficients vanish modulo that prime.
Suppose that d is good and that the positive integer divisor e divides d. The d roots of Xd−1 form a finite multiplicative subgroup H of Fp×​. By the fact that every finite multiplicative subgroup of a field is cyclic, H=⟨g⟩ is a cyclic group of order d. The solutions in H of xe=1 are
1,gd/e,g2d/e,…,g(e−1)d/e,
(1)
so there are at least e of them. The Lagrange root bound over a field gives at most e roots in all of Fp​, hence exactly e. Thus every divisor of a good number is good.
Now put n=pq. By the Chinese remainder theorem for unit groups, a base b is a Fermat-pseudoprime base precisely when its two components satisfy
bn−1=1in Fp×​andbn−1=1in Fq×​.
(2)
The power roots in a finite field and
gcd(n−1,p−1)=gcd(q−1,p−1)=10,gcd(n−1,q−1)=gcd(p−1,q−1)=10
(3)
show that each component has ten choices. Therefore there are
10⋅10=100
(4)
Fermat-pseudoprime bases.
To impose the strong pseudoprime condition, write n−1=2sm with m odd. Since 10∣n−1, we have 5∣m. In each cyclic group of ten Fermat components, raising to the mth power sends five elements to 1 and five elements to −1. A pair of components passes the strong test exactly when their signs agree: the pair (1,1) satisfies the first alternative, and (−1,−1) satisfies the second at j=0. Components of opposite sign become (1,1) after squaring and can never jointly equal −1. Hence the number of strong-pseudoprime bases is
52+52=50.
(5)

2F OurBigBook.com
For a continuous closed path γ:[0,1]→C∖{0}, choose a continuous argument lift
∣γ(t)∣γ(t)​=e2πiθ(t).
(6)
Its winding number of a continuous closed path about zero is
w(γ,0)=θ(1)−θ(0)∈Z.
(7)
For a piecewise smooth path this equals (2πi)−1∫γ​dz/z.
If ∣γ(t)∣>∣ϕ(t)∣, then
H(s,t)=γ(t)+sϕ(t),0≤s≤1,
(8)
never vanishes, since ∣H(s,t)∣≥∣γ(t)∣−s∣ϕ(t)∣>0. Thus H is a homotopy through closed paths avoiding zero. By homotopy invariance of winding number, or directly by the dominated-perturbation lemma,
w(γ+ϕ,0)=w(γ,0).
(9)
More generally, γ0​ and γ1​ are homotopic by paths in Γ when there is a continuous function
H:[0,1]2⟶C∖{0}
(10)
with H(0,t)=γ0​(t), H(1,t)=γ1​(t), and H(s,0)=H(s,1) for every s. The winding-number theorem states that such a homotopy implies
w(γ0​,0)=w(γ1​,0).
(11)
For the Fundamental theorem of algebra, let P(z)=an​zn+⋯+a0​ with n≥1. For sufficiently large R,
∣an​Rne2πint∣>∣an−1​Rn−1e2πi(n−1)t+⋯+a0​∣
(12)
for every t. The dominated-perturbation lemma shows that t↦P(Re2πit) has the same winding number as t↦an​Rne2πint, namely n. If P had no zero, however,
H(s,t)=P(sRe2πit)
(13)
would be a homotopy in Γ from that loop to the constant loop P(0), whose winding number is zero. This contradiction proves that P has a complex root. This is the winding-number proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra.
Finally suppose that a continuous retraction r:D2→S1 existed. The boundary loop η(t)=e2πit has winding number one, while (1−s)η(t) contracts it to zero inside the disc. Composing this contraction with r gives a homotopy through loops in S1 from r∘η=η to the constant loop r(0). Their winding numbers are respectively one and zero, contradicting homotopy invariance. Hence there is no such retraction, as in the winding-number proof of the no-retraction theorem.

i OurBigBook.com
A Bernoulli source is a sequence (Xn​)n≥1​ of independent and identically distributed random variables with a common probability mass function on the finite alphabet A.
The source is reliably encodable at rate r if, for each block length n, there are an encoder with at most 2nr outputs and a decoder such that the block error probability
P(X1n​=X1n​)
(14)
tends to zero as n→∞.
Its information rate is the limiting information entropy per source symbol,
h=limn→∞​n1​H(X1​,…,Xn​),
(15)
when this limit exists.

ii OurBigBook.com
For a Bernoulli source, independence makes entropy additive, so
H(X1​,…,Xn​)=∑j=1n​H(Xj​)=nH(X1​).
(16)
Its information rate is therefore H(X1​). If c is an optimal prefix code and L(c)=E∣c(X1​)∣ is its expected codeword length, the Shannon noiseless coding theorem gives
H(X1​)≤L(c)<H(X1​)+1.
(17)
Consequently the information rate is at most the expected word length of the optimal code.

The first m letters of the blocked source contain exactly the first mN letters of the original source, so
H(Y1​,…,Ym​)=H(X1​,…,XmN​).

limm→∞​m1​H(Y1​,…,Ym​)=Nlimm→∞​mN1​H(X1​,…,XmN​)=Nh.
(19)
Thus fixed-length blocking multiplies information rate by N, exactly as recorded by information rate under fixed-length blocking.

Suppose A=ranf for a partial computable function f. Since A=∅, fix a0​∈A. Decode each input w as a pair ((w)0​,(w)1​)=(u,t). Using the truncated computation function, define
h(w)={f(u),a0​,​if the computation of f(u) halts within t steps,otherwise.​
(22)
This is a total computable function, and every output lies in A. Conversely, if a=f(u), choosing t at least the halting time gives an input w with h(w)=a. Thus ranh=A, proving (iii)⇒(iv).

Suppose A=ranh for a total computable function h. Effectively enumerate the words as w0​,w1​,…. On input x, compute
h(w0​),h(w1​),…
(23)
in order and halt as soon as one equals x. Every individual computation terminates because h is total. The search halts exactly for x∈ranh=A, so A is computably enumerable. This proves (iv)⇒(i) and completes the equivalence recorded by the domain and range characterizations of a nonempty computably enumerable set.

5J OurBigBook.com
The commands choose n=100 observations and p=2 predictors; generate a 100×2 matrix X of independent standard-normal values; generate independent binary random variables Yi​ with success probability 1/2; and report the observed number of successes, ∑i​Yi​=48. The first glm call then fits the Bernoulli logistic-regression model
Yi​∼Bernoulli(pi​),log1−pi​pi​​=β0​+β1​Xi1​+β2​Xi2​.
(24)
The prediction command returns the fitted response probabilities p​i​ and sums them.
The likelihood is
L(β)=∏i=1100​piYi​​(1−pi​)1−Yi​,pi​=1+eηi​eηi​​,ηi​=β0​+β1​Xi1​+β2​Xi2​.
(25)
At the maximum-likelihood estimator, the intercept component of the score function is
0=∂β0​∂logL​=∑i=1100​(Yi​−p​i​).
(26)
Therefore
∑i​p​i​=∑i​Yi​=48
(27)
exactly, by the fitted-mean balance for logistic regression with an intercept.
The second fit uses probit regression,
pi​=Φ(ηi​),
(28)
where Φ is the standard normal distribution function. Its intercept score is
∑i​pi​(1−pi​)ϕ(ηi​)​(Yi​−pi​)=0,
(29)
a weighted residual equation. It does not imply ∑i​p​i​=48, so exact equality is not expected. The output should nevertheless be close to 48: the data were generated with constant success probability 1/2 independently of X, so the fitted slopes should be small, the linear predictors should cluster near a common intercept, and the score weights should be nearly constant.

Solution

Words: 89
a OurBigBook.com
This is the SIR model with waning immunity. The mass-action interaction term βIS transfers people from the susceptible compartment to the infected compartment, νI transfers infectives to the recovered compartment, and fR returns recovered people to susceptibility as immunity wanes. Adding the equations gives
dtd​(S+I+R)=0,
(30)
so the total population N is conserved.
When f=0 and infection is rare, S≃N and
I′=(βS−ν)I≃(βN−ν)I.
(31)
Thus I initially decays if βN<ν. Equivalently, the basic reproduction number is R0​=βN/ν<1, so the epidemic invasion threshold is not crossed and no epidemic occurs.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

b

Words: 168 Articles: 1
6C OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 168
b OurBigBook.com
At a nontrivial equilibrium I∗>0, the equation I′=0 gives
S∗=βν​.
(32)
The equation R′=0 gives R∗=νI∗/f, and conservation of population then yields
I∗=β(f+ν)f(βN−ν)​,R∗=β(f+ν)ν(βN−ν)​.
(33)
These values are positive precisely in the epidemic regime βN>ν.
Eliminate R=N−S−I. The two-dimensional system is
S′=f(N−S−I)−βIS,I′=(βS−ν)I.
(34)
Set a=βI∗=f(βN−ν)/(f+ν)>0. The Jacobian matrix at the endemic equilibrium is
J=(−(f+a)a​−(f+ν)0​),
(35)
so its eigenvalues satisfy
λ2+(f+a)λ+a(f+ν)=0.
(36)
Their sum is −(f+a)<0 and their product is a(f+ν)>0, proving local asymptotic stability.
The discriminant is
Δ=(f+a)2−4a(f+ν).
(37)
Writing r=βN−ν>0, we have a=fr/(f+ν). As f→0+,
Δ=−4fr+O(f2)<0,
(38)
whereas as f→∞,
Δ=f2−2rf+O(1)>0.
(39)
Hence sufficiently slow immunity loss gives a stable focus: I(t) approaches I∗ through damped oscillations, corresponding to successively smaller epidemic waves. Sufficiently rapid immunity loss gives a stable node: small disturbances are sums of two decaying real modes and show no forced oscillation. These conclusions and the equilibrium formulas are collected in the Endemic equilibrium of the SIR model with waning immunity.

For ℜs>1, absolute convergence permits separation into odd and even terms:
n=1∑∞​(−1)n−1n−s​=n=1∑∞​n−s−2n=1∑∞​(2n)−s=(1−21−s)ζ(s).​
(40)
Using the defining integral of the Gamma function and the substitution u=nt gives
Γ(s)n−s=∫0∞​ts−1e−ntdt.
(41)
Termwise integration is justified by absolute convergence when ℜs>1, and the geometric sum is
∑n=1∞​(−1)n−1e−nt=1+et1​.
(42)
Consequently the Dirichlet eta function satisfies
(1−21−s)ζ(s)=η(s)=Γ(s)1​∫0∞​1+etts−1​dt.
(43)
Near zero the integrand is O(tℜs−1), while at infinity it decays exponentially. The integral therefore defines a holomorphic function for ℜs>0. Thus
ζ(s)=(1−21−s)Γ(s)1​∫0∞​1+etts−1​dt​
(44)
provides the desired continuation wherever the displayed denominator is nonzero. At a nonreal zero of 1−21−s, use instead
(1−k1−s)ζ(s)=∑n≥1​an​n−s,an​={1,1−k,​k∤n,k∣n,​
(45)
with an integer k for which 1−k1−s=0; the bounded partial sums of an​ give convergence for ℜs>0. This shows that those apparent singularities are removable and yields the Analytic continuation of the Riemann zeta function to the right half-plane.
At s=1,
η(1)=∫0∞​1+etdt​=log2,
(46)
whereas
1−21−s=1−e−(s−1)log2=(s−1)log2+O((s−1)2).
(47)
Hence
ζ(s)=s−11​+O(1),
(48)
so s=1 is a simple pole and its residue is
Ress=1​ζ(s)=1​.
(49)

Solution

Words: 140
8D OurBigBook.com
A fixed space frame is an inertial orthonormal frame whose axes remain fixed in space. A principal body frame is attached to the rigid body and aligned with the principal axes of its inertia tensor, so that the tensor is diagonal with entries I1​,I2​,I3​.
If ei​(t) are the body axes and ω is the angular velocity, then the derivative of a body-fixed basis vector is
e˙i​=ω×ei​.
(50)
In the principal frame,
L=∑i=13​Ii​ωi​ei​.
(51)
For torque-free motion, the angular momentum has zero space derivative. Therefore
0=dtdL​=∑i​Ii​ω˙i​ei​+ω×L.
(52)
Taking body-frame components gives the Euler equations for a torque-free rigid body:
I1​ω˙1​I2​ω˙2​I3​ω˙3​​=(I2​−I3​)ω2​ω3​,=(I3​−I1​)ω3​ω1​,=(I1​−I2​)ω1​ω2​.​
(53)
For an axisymmetric body, put I1​=I2​=I and let e3​ be its symmetry axis. Decompose ω=ω1​e1​+ω2​e2​+ω3​e3​. Then
L​=Iω1​e1​+Iω2​e2​+I3​ω3​e3​=Iω+(I3​−I)ω3​e3​.​
(54)
Thus L is a linear combination of ω and e3​, proving that the angular momentum, angular velocity, and symmetry axis are always coplanar. This is the coplanarity in a torque-free axisymmetric rigid body.

x=kB​Thν​,dν=hkB​T​dx.

Then
n=c38π​(hkB​​)3T3∫0∞​ex−1x2​dx=αT3,

where
α=c38π​(hkB​​)3∫0∞​ex−1x2​dx.

Each photon of frequency ν has energy hν, so the energy density is
ρ​=c38πh​∫0∞​ehν/(kB​T)−1ν3​dν=c3h38πkB4​​T4∫0∞​ex−1x3​dx=ξT4.​
(58)
This is the temperature scaling of thermal photon number and energy densities.
After decoupling, cosmological redshift gives
ν(t)=a(t)a(tdec​)​νdec​,νdec​=a(tdec​)a(t)​ν(t).
(59)
The occupation number is conserved along the freely propagating photon trajectory. Its exponential argument at decoupling becomes
kB​Tdec​hνdec​​=kB​(a(tdec​)Tdec​/a(t))hν(t)​.

The Baire category theorem states that every countable intersection of open dense subsets of a complete metric space is dense. Equivalently, no nonempty open subset of a complete metric space is a countable union of nowhere dense sets.
To prove the first form, let G1​,G2​,… be open dense subsets of a complete metric space X, and let V⊆X be nonempty and open. Choose a closed ball
B(x1​,r1​)⊆V∩G1​,0<r1​<2−1.
(67)
Inductively, density and openness of Gn+1​ allow a closed ball
B(xn+1​,rn+1​)⊆B(xn​,rn​)∩Gn+1​,0<rn+1​<2−(n+1).
(68)
The balls are nested and d(xm​,xn​)<2−n for m>n, so (xn​) is Cauchy. Completeness gives xn​→x∈X. For every n, all later centres lie in B(xn​,rn​); closedness gives x∈B(xn​,rn​)⊆Gn​. The first ball also lies in V, hence
x∈V∩⋂n=1∞​Gn​.
(69)
Since every nonempty open V meets the intersection, that intersection is dense.

A one-time pad over the finite additive group Zn​ uses a key K that is uniform on Zn​, independent of the plaintext X, as long as the plaintext, and never reused. Encryption and decryption are
C=X+K(modn),X=C−K(modn).
(80)
For independent random variables X,Y, conditioning reduces entropy and translation by a known element of the finite additive group preserves entropy, so
H(X+Y)≥H(X+Y∣Y)=H(X∣Y)=H(X).
(81)
Interchanging X and Y gives H(X+Y)≥H(Y), hence
H(X+Y)≥max{H(X),H(Y)}​.
(82)
This is the entropy of a sum of independent finite-group variables.
The result explains why adding independent pad symbols cannot reduce uncertainty. For a uniform pad, X+K is itself uniform and is independent of X, which is the perfect-secrecy property. Independence is necessary: if X is nonconstant and Y=−X(modn), then X+Y=0 is constant, so
H(X+Y)=0<H(X)=H(Y).
(83)

We prove that this counting function is a polynomial by induction on the number of edges. If G has n vertices and no edges, every assignment of colours is proper, so

PG​(t)=PG−e​(t)−PG/e​(t).

Now consider connected finite covers of the closed orientable surface Σg​. By the classification of connected covering spaces, degree-n connected covers correspond to index-n subgroups of the fundamental group of a closed orientable surface, and normal covers correspond to normal subgroups.

If F:X→Y is a nonconstant holomorphic map between compact connected Riemann surfaces, its local degree at p is the integer mF​(p)≥1 for which suitable local coordinates give
F(z)−F(p)=azmF​(p)+O(zmF​(p)+1),a=0.
(272)
The valency theorem states that
∑p∈F−1(y)​mF​(p)
(273)
is independent of y∈Y. This common value is the degree of a holomorphic map, denoted degF.
Now let f be a nonconstant rational function of degree d. If its distinct finite poles have orders m1​,…,mr​, and its pole order at infinity is m∞​≥0, then
d=m1​+⋯+mr​+m∞​.
(274)
The derivative f′ has a pole of order mj​+1 at each finite pole. When m∞​>0, the expansion f(z)∼czm∞​ shows that f′(z)∼cm∞​zm∞​−1 at infinity. Hence the degree of the derivative of a rational function is
degf′={d+r−1,d+r,​m∞​>0,m∞​=0.​
(275)
In the first case r≥0, while in the second 1≤r≤d; therefore
d−1≤degf′≤2d.​
(276)
For every d≥1, the lower bound is attained by f(z)=zd, whose derivative has degree d−1 (with a constant assigned degree zero). For distinct a1​,…,ad​, the function
f(z)=∑j=1d​z−aj​1​
(277)
has d simple poles, degree d, and a derivative with d double poles, so degf′=2d. Thus both rational bounds are sharp for every d.
Let next g be a nonconstant elliptic function for the period lattice Λ. Its degree is the total order of its poles in a fundamental parallelogram; by the valency theorem, this is also the degree of the induced map C/Λ→C. If these poles have orders n1​,…,ns​, then d=degg=∑j​nj​, and g′ has poles of orders nj​+1. The degree of the derivative of an elliptic function is consequently
degg′=d+s.
(278)
Since every nonconstant elliptic function has at least one pole and 1≤s≤d,
d+1≤degg′≤2d.​
(279)
Let d≥3 be odd. The Weierstrass elliptic function supplies the lower-bound example
g(z)=℘(z)(d−3)/2℘′(z).
(280)
It has one pole modulo Λ, of order d, so its derivative has one pole of order d+1. For the upper bound, choose distinct points a1​,…,ad​ modulo Λ and nonzero constants cj​ with ∑j​cj​=0. The quasi-periodicity of the Weierstrass zeta function makes
g(z)=∑j=1d​cj​ζ(z−aj​)
(281)
elliptic. It has exactly d simple poles, while g′ has d double poles. Therefore the two bounds are attained for every required odd degree.

ℓ(D)−ℓ(KX​−D)=degD+1−g,

where KX​ is a canonical divisor. Taking D=0 gives 1−ℓ(KX​)=1−g, so ℓ(KX​)=g. Taking D=KX​ then gives
g−1=degKX​+1−g,degKX​=2g−2​.

To obtain a uniform projective embedding, choose a divisor D of degree 2g+1. Since every divisor appearing below has degree greater than 2g−2, Riemann--Roch gives
ℓ(D)=g+2,ℓ(D−P)=g+1,ℓ(D−P−Q)=g,ℓ(D−2P)=g.
(284)
The first two equalities show that the complete linear system of a divisor ∣D∣ has no base point. The strict drops in the last two comparisons show respectively that its sections separate distinct points P,Q and tangent directions at P. Thus D is a very ample divisor, in accordance with the general fact that a high-degree divisor is very ample on a smooth projective curve, and its sections define a closed embedding
X↪Pℓ(D)−1=Pg+1.​
(285)
The ambient dimension therefore depends only on g.
The Riemann-Hurwitz formula for a nonconstant morphism h:C1​→C2​ of degree n is
2g(C1​)−2=n(2g(C2​)−2)+∑P∈C1​​(eP​−1).

Choose a smooth plane quartic C, so g(C)=3, and form the product of projective varieties S=C×C. This is a smooth projective variety of dimension two. If B⊂S is an irreducible curve, pass to its normalization B. At least one coordinate projection B→C is nonconstant, since otherwise B would be a point. For that projection, Riemann--Hurwitz gives
2g(B)−2≥n(2⋅3−2)≥4,
(287)
so the geometric genus of B is at least three. Hence S is the required surface; this is the product surface without low-genus curves construction.

[x:y:z]⟼[x:y].

degRπ​=2g(X)−2+2d=(d−1)(d−2)−2+2d=d(d−1).

Every ramification point contributes at least one to this degree, so

For x˙=f(x), a fixed point x∗ satisfies f(x∗)=0. It is Lyapunov stable when, for every ε>0, there is δ>0 such that
∣x(0)−x∗∣<δ⟹∣x(t)−x∗∣<ε(t≥0).
(373)
A Lyapunov function on a neighbourhood of x∗ is a continuously differentiable function V such that
V(x∗)=0,V(x)>0(x=x∗),V˙(x)=∇V(x)⋅f(x)≤0.
(374)
The First Lyapunov theorem states that such a function makes x∗ Lyapunov stable. If V˙<0 away from x∗, then x∗ is locally asymptotically stable.
To prove stability, choose a closed ball contained in the domain of V. On its boundary sphere ∣x−x∗∣=ε, compactness and positive definiteness give
m=min∣x−x∗∣=ε​V(x)>0.
(375)
Continuity at x∗ supplies δ<ε such that ∣x−x∗∣<δ implies V(x)<m. Along a trajectory, V cannot increase. Such a trajectory therefore cannot first reach the boundary sphere, where its value would be at least m. This proves Lyapunov stability.
If V˙<0 away from x∗, take a sufficiently small compact sublevel set of V. The LaSalle invariance principle says that every trajectory in it approaches the largest invariant subset of {V˙=0}, which is just {x∗}. Hence the equilibrium is also asymptotically stable.

The Navier-Stokes equation for constant mass density ρ, dynamic viscosity μ, and body force per unit mass f is
ρ(∂t​u+u⋅∇u)=∇⋅σ+ρf,∇⋅u=0,
(456)
where the Newtonian fluid stress tensor is
σ=−pI+2μe,e=21​(∇u+(∇u)T).
(457)
Taking the dot product with u gives
ρu⋅(∂t​u+u⋅∇u)=∇⋅(σu)−σ:∇u+ρf⋅u.
(458)
Incompressibility implies
σ:∇u=2μe:e,
(459)
and converts the left side into a local time derivative plus the divergence of kinetic-energy flux. The divergence theorem therefore gives the kinetic-energy balance for an incompressible Newtonian fluid
dtd​∫Ω​21​ρ∣u∣2dV=​−∫∂Ω​21​ρ∣u∣2u⋅ndS+∫∂Ω​u⋅σndS+∫Ω​ρf⋅udV−2μ∫Ω​e:edV.​​
(460)
The four terms are respectively outward advective transport of kinetic energy, mechanical power supplied by surface traction, power supplied by the body force, and irreversible viscous dissipation into heat.

Let a denote the bubble size, U its speed, and Re=Ua/ν≫1 the Reynolds number. Outside a thin boundary layer, inertia dominates and the flow is an irrotational flow with velocity scale U and strain scale U/a. Its viscous dissipation has order
Douter​∼μ(aU​)2a3∼μU2a
(461)
in three dimensions.
The boundary-layer thickness is
δ∼(Uνa​)1/2=aRe−1/2.
(462)
For a clean bubble the stress-free boundary condition prescribes tangential stress rather than tangential velocity. The outer flow already has tangential strain of order U/a, so cancelling that stress requires a velocity correction of only
Δu∼aU​δ,
(463)
not a correction of order U. Its gradient remains O(U/a), and its boundary-layer dissipation is
Dlayer​∼μ(aU​)2a2δ∼Douter​aδ​,
(464)
which is asymptotically smaller.
In steady translation, the drag power DU balances viscous dissipation. The leading estimate therefore follows from the known outer flow alone:
D∼UDouter​​∼μUa​
(465)
in three dimensions. This is the dissipation estimate for high-Reynolds-number bubble drag.

ϕ=−U(r+ra2​)cosθ​.
(466)
It is harmonic for r>a and gives
ur​=−U(1−r2a2​)cosθ,uθ​=U(1+r2a2​)sinθ.​
(467)
Thus ur​=0 on r=a, satisfying the kinematic boundary condition, and u→−Uex​ as r→∞. The laboratory-frame flow is obtained by adding Uex​.

err​=−r32Ua2​cosθ,eθθ​=r32Ua2​cosθ,erθ​=−r32Ua2​sinθ.
(468)
Therefore
e:e=err2​+eθθ2​+2erθ2​=r68U2a4​.

D​=2μ∫a∞​∫02π​e:erdθdr=16μU2a4(2π)∫a∞​r−5dr=8πμU2.​

c OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 97
iii OurBigBook.com
A rigid body obeys the no-slip boundary condition. Its outer potential flow generally has an O(U) tangential slip velocity at the surface, so the boundary layer must make an O(U) velocity correction across thickness δ. Its strain is therefore O(U/δ), and in two dimensions its dissipation per unit axial length is
Dlayer​∼μ(δU​)2aδ=μU2δa​,
(472)
which exceeds the O(μU2) outer dissipation by a/δ∼Re1/2.
The dominant drag consequently depends on the detailed boundary-layer velocity field and possibly on boundary-layer separation. It cannot be obtained by integrating the outer irrotational strain alone.

Let kS​=ω/cS​ and kP​=ω/cP​. Snell law for elastic waves fixes the reflected waves' common tangential wavenumber:
kS​sinθ=kP​sinϕ,sinϕ=cS​cP​​sinθ.

Choose the reflected SV-wave and converted reflected P-wave as
uRS​=Re{R(cosθ,0,sinθ)eikS​(xsinθ−zcosθ)−iωt},
(474)
uRP​=Re{T(sinϕ,0,−cosϕ)eikP​(xsinϕ−zcosϕ)−iωt}.

The polarizations are respectively perpendicular and parallel to their wavevectors. Phase matching makes all three exponential factors equal at z=0. The rigid boundary condition for an elastic wave uI​+uRS​+uRP​=0 there gives
cosθ(1+R)+Tsinϕ=0,
(476)
−sinθ+Rsinθ−Tcosϕ=0.
(477)

R=−cos(θ−ϕ)cos(θ+ϕ)​​,T=−cos(θ−ϕ)sin2θ​​.

These fields give the Reflection of an SV-wave from a rigid plane.

sinϕ=cS​cP​​sinθ,

sinθ>cP​cS​​​.

s=cS​cP​​sinθ>1,q=s2−1​,cosϕ=iq.

⟨Pz​⟩=−21​Re(σzj​u˙j∗​).

The matrix C from part (a) is Hermitian positive definite, while the real diagonal matrix D is Hermitian. The stated product theorem, or similarity
CD=C1/2(C1/2DC1/2)C−1/2,
(499)
shows that every eigenvalue of CD is real. Hence every eigenvalue of B=−CD is real; this is the real spectrum of a positive-Hermitian times Hermitian product.
Moreover, C is invertible and D has rank 2d, so for d≥1 the matrix B has nonzero real eigenvalues. If λ=0 is one of them, the corresponding mode of the semidiscrete equation has eigenvalue iπλ. The explicit Euler method has amplification factor
G=1+iπλΔt,∣G∣=1+π2λ2Δt2​>1
(500)
for every Δt>0. Therefore the explicit Euler discretization is unstable, as in explicit Euler instability on a nonzero imaginary eigenvalue.
